note: The imperfective past here is a plain report, not an action viewed from inside; English uses the simple past for that, and the progressive needs a frame ("when …") the sentence does not supply.

en: They performed in front of the audience.
note: The imperfective past here is a plain report, not an action viewed from inside; English uses the simple past for that, and the progressive needs a frame ("when …") the sentence does not supply.
en_alt: They were performing in front of the audience.

en: They discussed the plans for a long time.
note: With an explicit duration English takes the simple past — the progressive fights «до́лго»/«два го́да» rather than rendering it.

en: He spent a long time repairing the old car.
note: English does not put a duration on a simple past of a durative activity — "repaired it for a long time" suggests the repair completed. "Spent a long time -ing" is how the imperfective + «до́лго» is said.
en_alt: He repaired the old car for a long time.

en: The workers spent two years building the bridge.
note: Same shape: «два го́да» is the span of the activity, not of a completed build, and "built the bridge for two years" reads as a finished bridge that lasted two years.
en_alt: The workers built the bridge for two years.

en: Yesterday we were reading an interesting story.
note: Reverses this stage's own earlier call, which restored the simple past because «вчера́» anchors the sentence to a completed time. That is right about the English read alone, and it is not how this English is used: the verb-contrast drill shows it by itself and asks чита́ть or прочита́ть, and a bare past "read" is aspect-neutral, so the item had two right answers — the collision packet-089 closed on exactly these grounds and this stage re-opened. A learner reported it (#611). The progressive leads again and the simple past becomes an accepted alternate, so the word-bank drill still credits the natural rendering while the contrast drill has a cue to read.
en_alt: Yesterday we read an interesting story.
